vignette: The first strike comes without warning, a sharp crack against his jaw that echoes in Samir’s memory like a dropped pot. He is thirty-eight, newly married, and standing in the kitchen of their first apartment when his partner’s hand connects with his face. The violence unfolds over the next fourteen months like a slow tide. It begins as correction, disguised as discipline, but quickly settles into a rhythm: a broken collarbone from a thrown lamp, a bruised rib from a shove against the counter, a fractured wrist when he attempts to block a backhand. He learns to read the air before it thickens, to swallow his words before they spark an escalation. He never calls the police. In the cultural framework of his parents’ homeland, in the unspoken codes of his family, a man does not air his household wars. He sleeps with one eye open, his keys always within reach, his phone charged, bracing for the next threshold. When he finally leaves, he carries the architecture of that terror with him. At fifty-four, he still maps every room before he sits. His eyes track the exits, linger on door handles, settle on the window behind the clinician. He arrives to sessions early, posture rigid, hands clasped around a cold coffee cup. When the clock ticks past the half-hour mark, his shoulders hike toward his ears. He does not notice a pen resting too close to his knee. His work as a community organizer once demanded that he stand in front of angry crowds, negotiate with city officials, and hold space for collective grief. He still does that work, but his body has learned a different script. During a coalition meeting yesterday, a colleague accidentally drops a heavy binder. Samir flinches so violently he knocks over his water glass. He spends the next twenty minutes apologizing to the wet floor, his breathing shallow, his mind trapped in the geometry of that kitchen. He tells me later that he feels like an imposter in his own life. He still attends neighborhood rallies, but his voice has lost its bottom register. He avoids eye contact, rehearses conversations in his head before speaking, and leaves events early. He has stopped attending tenant dinners, citing workload, but the truth is simpler: he cannot bear the sound of a chair scraping against tile. His marriage endures, but the distance between them has become a quiet geography he no longer knows how to cross. His wife cooks his favorite meals, folds his shirts, asks gentle questions he cannot answer. He loves her fiercely, but he wakes at 3 a.m., his chest tight, his body sweating as if still bracing for impact. He lies beside her, listening to her steady breathing, guilt sitting in his throat like a stone. He thinks he failed the men he mentors, the elders he advises, the boys in the community center he helps lead after school. He wonders if the violence followed him out the door, or if he carried it in his bones all along. When our hour ends, he stands slowly, smoothing his trousers. He thanks the clinician, his voice quiet but precise. He walks to the door, pauses, and looks back. “I keep waiting for the other shoe to drop,” he says, almost to himself. Then he steps into the hallway, his footsteps measured, his shoulders still set against the wind.
